A complainant, a sole-trader's car owner, objected to a personalised number plate of his car being shown for minutes in a Belgian TV fiction episode about a drug gang, and asked for its removal, which the broadcaster refused on artistic-freedom grounds. The Litigation Chamber found that, in these specific circumstances, the plate was personal data because people around the complainant could identify him through it. It then dismissed the main infringements of the accountability, data protection by design, erasure and DPO provisions, dismissed the Article 12(1) finding without further action, and issued a warning on the transparency duty in Article 12(4). No fine was imposed.

Following a lack of substantive feedback or assessment from the DPC during the mutual assistance procedure (Article 61 GDPR), The Italian DPA initiated the urgency mechanism in Article 66 GDPR to prohibit Meta’s processing of personal data in the context of the Italian elections.

A neighbour complained about cameras at a guesthouse that filmed their property, and the authority also opened its own investigation into the guesthouse's camera systems. It found that the operating company unlawfully processed the complainant's data and unlawfully filmed the jacuzzi, restaurant and inner courtyard. It also found excessive storage, poor and hard-to-reach information to data subjects, and failure to cooperate with the authority. The company was ordered to remove the cameras, delete the recordings, fix its information practice, and pay a HUF 3,000,000 fine. The proceedings against the property owner were terminated.

The Bulgarian DPA fined a doctor BGN 500 (approx. €255) for a violation of Article 32 GDPR. The Doctor had allowed that her electronic signature was used to access the vaccination status of a member of the European Parliament. This information was later disclosed in a television programme.

The Irish DPC conducted an own-volition inquiry into a care provider after breaches in which a manager's email account was accessed by a third party and a forwarding rule sent personal data, including residents' health data, to an external address. It found that the company failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures, infringing Article 5(1)(f) GDPR, and that this was negligent. It ordered the company to bring its processing into compliance within 90 days, issued a reprimand, and imposed a fine of €100,000. The fine was calculated against the combined turnover of the company and its ultimate parent.

A survey participant asked the polling company for a copy of a recorded call with its representative and got no answer. The company said its retention policy had already deleted the data, but it did not inform the complainant of that or explain how rights requests are handled. The Authority found a breach of the right of access under Article 15 read with Article 12(1), (3) and (4) GDPR. It issued a reprimand and ordered the company to set up procedures for data subject rights within two months. The first, related complaint was withdrawn and filed away. No fine was imposed.

France's CNIL restricted committee fined a US technology group's French-market search advertising entity, whose name is redacted in the text, for placing advertising cookies on users' terminals in France without prior consent, breaching the French Article 82 rule (the national transposition of the ePrivacy Directive's Article 5(3)). The procedure began with a complaint filed on 21 February 2020, followed by online inspections in 2020 and 2021. The committee imposed an administrative fine of EUR 60 million, ordered the company to obtain consent before advertising-fraud cookies are placed, set a penalty of EUR 60,000 per day of delay after three months, and ordered publication of the decision.

A former employee complained that his employer sent an email to the whole workplace, and to a wider group, explaining that he had been dismissed for cooperation difficulties and giving detailed background. The employer argued this was needed to prevent rumours. Datatilsynet held that the information about the dismissal went beyond what was necessary for informing the relevant people, so the processing did not comply with Article 6(1) GDPR. It issued a criticism (reprimand) without a fine.

A customer of a slimming and aesthetics business complained that the company ignored her written and extrajudicial requests for copies of her contracts, records of sessions attended and a statement of her surplus balance. The company also failed to answer the Authority's repeated requests for its views over more than a year, replying only after a hearing. The Authority found that access was granted late and incompletely (Articles 12(3) and 15) and that the company breached the duty to cooperate (Article 31). It fined the company EUR 2,000 and EUR 5,000 respectively and ordered it to satisfy the outstanding access request.

The Dutch DPA (AP) reprimanded CAK, a Dutch public body, for violation of Article 12(3) GDPR because CAK did not respond in a timely manner to an access request. The AP concluded a reprimand is a fitting sanction since the breach was small.

A complainant objected that the embassy of the Republic of N*** in Vienna posted a voter list showing his name, date of birth and voter register number on the outside of its building during the 2022 elections. The Austrian DSB held that, under Article 55 GDPR, it is competent for processing on Austrian territory, but that the embassy's processing is not within its reach because diplomatic immunity under the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations (Art. 31) bars enforcement against the mission. The complaint was rejected (zurückgewiesen).

The Romanian DPA closed an investigation in November 2022 into Societatea Energetică Electrica S.A., which started after the company notified a personal data breach. It found a violation of Article 28(3)(a) GDPR and fined the company 24,654.50 lei (about EUR 5,000). It also recommended that the controller take all necessary measures to comply with Articles 46-49 GDPR on transfers. The text is a short press release, not the full decision.

A patient complained that at the Recoletas clinic in Ponferrada the data-protection consent boxes on the admission tablet (third-party sharing and marketing) were pre-ticked by staff. He also complained that he never received a copy of the form he signed. The AEPD opened sanction proceedings and proposed two fines of EUR 10,000 each, one for Article 6(1) GDPR (defective consent) and one for Article 15 with Article 12 GDPR (no access to the signed document). The hospital paid EUR 16,000 on 31 October 2022 using the 20% reduction for voluntary payment, which ended the procedure. By paying it waived any administrative appeal.

The Garante investigated the stratification of patients by risk (using the Johns Hopkins ACG algorithm, RUB 4 and 5 classes) carried out under a regional resolution for Covid-19 proactive medicine, with lists sent to general practitioners. Health data of over 40,000 patients, 9,487 of them from the Friuli Occidentale health authority, were processed. The Garante found no valid legal basis, no specific information to data subjects and no data protection impact assessment. It declared the processing unlawful, fined the authority EUR 55,000 and ordered deletion of the resulting data within 90 days. A later note says the Tribunal of Pordenone annulled the decision on 13 October 2023.

The Italian DPA fined a health authority €55,000 for the unlawful processing of special category health data. The controller sought to compile a list of patients vulnerable to major complications from Covid-19 infection.

A public lower secondary school published on its electronic register a class-by-class list of pupils requesting in-person or remote lessons, with acronyms (BES, DSA, ALUNNO H) next to some names that reveal health-related information. The list was visible to the class's teachers and families for about 18 hours before removal. The Garante found the disclosure unlawful under Articles 5, 6 and 9 GDPR and the Italian Code (articles 2-ter and 2-sexies, pre-2021 version), and found a breach of Article 12 for failing to answer the families' rights request. It imposed a fine of EUR 3,000 and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website.

The municipality of Borgia informed the Garante that it was installing fingerprint-based systems to record employee attendance. The Garante found that it had processed employees' biometric data without a valid legal basis, contrary to the principle of lawfulness, and had failed to notify the Garante of the new data protection officer's contact details. The processing was a short trial of three days involving about 13 employees, and the system had been dismantled. Taking into account the small size of the municipality, its cooperation and its good faith, the Garante imposed a fine of EUR 5,000 and ordered publication of the decision. No corrective measures were ordered since the conduct had ended.

Following a report, the Garante investigated the municipality of Vicchio, which used fingerprint-based biometric time clocks to record employee attendance. The system was installed in 2020 relying on the 'Concretezza' law (Law 56/2019), whose biometric provisions were later repealed. The Garante found there was no adequate legal basis for processing employees' biometric data for attendance purposes, in breach of Articles 5, 6 and 9 GDPR, and rejected the municipality's claim of excusable error. It fined the municipality EUR 8,000 and ordered publication of the decision, with no corrective measures because the processing had ended and the data been deleted.

A former municipal employee complained that the municipality published on its online notice board a resolution taking note of her resignation and waiving the notice period. It identified her by initials, job role and employee number and referred to her health condition and drug therapy. The Garante found that this amounted to dissemination of personal and health data without a legal basis, and that initials plus context do not anonymise. It rejected the transparency-law justification. It declared the processing unlawful and fined the municipality EUR 6,000, with publication of the decision.

A lorry driver complained that he found a Visirun GPS tracker in his lorry, installed under a former employer's contract, and that his access request went unanswered. The Garante found that Verizon Connect Italy, the vehicle-tracking provider and processor, never had a written processor appointment under Article 28 with its customer, and that the location processing was unlawful under Articles 5(1)(a), 6 and 28. The processing ran from February 2016 to the end of 2020 and covered 76 devices. The Garante fined the company EUR 30,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

Following several complaints and reports about unwanted marketing calls made on behalf of Edison Energia, the Garante inspected the company in February 2022 and examined its telemarketing and profiling practices. It found that Edison used third-party contact lists without checks on consent, handled objections to marketing poorly (an incomplete do-not-contact list), and collected a single bundled consent for marketing and profiling on its website and app. The Garante declared the processing unlawful, banned further processing based on third-party lists lacking valid consent, and ordered corrective measures on checks, data subject rights and privacy notices. It fined the company EUR 4,900,000, equal to 0.1% of its latest turnover, and ordered publication of the decision.

A patient complained that an emergency-room record at the Policlinico Casilino, run by Eurosanità, was wrongly linked to a namesake patient with a different birth date, and the record ended up with the namesake. The company also notified a data breach. The Garante found that health data of both patients were processed unlawfully, breaching the principles of accuracy and integrity/confidentiality, Article 9 and Article 32 GDPR. It fined the company and ordered publication of the decision. The Rome Tribunal later reduced the fine to EUR 30,000 and upheld the publication (judgment 2648/2025 of 19 February 2025); the Garante's published text shows only the reduced amount.

An Italian doctor made critical statements concerning covid-19 health measures. The Provincial Order of Surgeons communicated, on TV and in a press release, information regarding disciplinary action against the doctor. The Italian DPA reprimanded the Order for violating Articles 5(1)(a) and 6 GDPR.

The Garante inspected Assiteca S.p.A., an insurance broker, in February and March 2022, after its planned inspection programme and some complaints. The inspection found that its car-insurance quote websites pre-ticked or wrongly recorded marketing consents, a system bug affected about 9,700 records and changed the consent of 2,155 users, consent for third-party and telemarketing use was not properly obtained, and no retention periods were set. The Garante had charged breaches of Articles 5(1)(a), (d), (e), 6(1)(a), 7, 13 and 24; in its assessment it found unlawful consent for marketing (Articles 6(1)(a) and 7, and Article 130 of the Code) and unlimited retention (Article 5(1)(e)), found the technical measures not fully adequate in the cases checked, and noted that the privacy notice had since been rewritten. It imposed a fine of EUR 120,000 and ordered publication of the decision on its website, without further corrective orders.

A delivery driver working for the furniture company complained that he found a GPS tracking device in the engine compartment of his truck, installed without information or valid consent. The Garante found that the company, as controller, processed location and mileage data of identifiable drivers through a device supplied by a telematics provider from 2016 to late 2020, even after the complainant's relationship ended. It found violations of transparency and lawfulness principles, the duty to inform, the processor-appointment requirement and the DPIA obligation. It fined the company EUR 50,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

The Greek DPA determined that the processing of personal data using a video surveillance camera in an apartment building was unlawful, after the general assembly of owners requested the removal of the device.

A data subject complained that Íslandsbanki sent statements of his mortgage debt position by post to other owners of flats in the same building. The bank argued the disclosure was required by the Icelandic Sureties Act, relying on the land-register owner list. The Icelandic DPA found the bank could not rely on that list alone, given the 27 registered owners and the unclear shares of 25 of them, so the disclosure had no legal basis and the bank had not shown appropriate security. It issued an order requiring measures to ensure appropriate security for such notices, with confirmation due by 23 January 2023. No fine was imposed.

The Luxemburg DPA fined Є3,700 to a company running a website and a mobile app for not providing sufficient information about the processing of data and for using a privacy policy that did not reflect reality.

Three complaints said Alektum Oy, a Finnish debt collector, did not answer data subject access requests, and the company also did not answer the supervisory authority's information requests. The Sanctions Board of the Office of the Data Protection Ombudsman found breaches of Article 15(1) and 15(3) and Article 12(3) GDPR. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 750,000 and, in addition, the Deputy Ombudsman issued a reprimand. The decision treats the non-response as a systematic practice and an aggravating factor.

Two co-owners of a residence complained that in February 2019 the company acting as syndic emailed other co-owners and a former co-owner a statement of one co-owner's account balance together with private home addresses, as a debt reminder. The complaints also concerned the handling of the co-owners' access requests. The Luxembourg CNPD (restricted formation) found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a), 6(1), 12(3) and (4) and 15(1)(b) and (c) GDPR and imposed a fine of EUR 1,500, below the EUR 2,500 proposed by the investigator. No corrective measures were imposed because the company no longer held the syndic mandate.

The Deputy Data Protection Ombudsman examined the Helmet library websites in the Helsinki capital region, which used tracking technologies such as Google Analytics and Matomo. The decision finds that the libraries had no valid legal basis for further processing of data collected by these trackers, that search data could leak to third parties (Google) through the referrer header, that users were not properly informed (including about transfers to the USA), and that there was no valid transfer basis for US transfers. The libraries were reprimanded and ordered to erase the data collected unlawfully and to bring processing into line with the GDPR; no order to stop processing was made because they had already started removing the trackers.

The Romanian authority finished an investigation in November 2022 into Casa Rusu S.R.L. after the company notified a personal data breach. An unauthorised form had been inserted into the online payment section of the company's website and collected customers' bank card data. The authority found that appropriate technical and organisational measures had not been implemented and that their effectiveness had not been regularly tested. It fined the company RON 9,883.60 (about EUR 2,000) and ordered it to review and update its technical and organisational measures.

A former employee complained that Viking Line kept employees' health data, including diagnoses, in an HR system for a long time, that some of it was wrong, and that the company did not give him all the data he asked for. The Deputy Data Protection Ombudsman found several failings: health data was handled unlawfully and inaccurately, employees were not properly informed, and the access request was not fully met. The deputy ombudsman ordered the company to bring its information practices into line with the GDPR and issued a reprimand. The sanctions board imposed an administrative fine of EUR 230,000 on the company.

The Estonian DPA held that, when responding requests for access to information, professional entities must carry out a thorough balancing exercise to assess whether the personal data they hold are of public interest or are covered by the inviolability of private life, justifying any restriction to the access to information.

A former employee complained that the company had not closed the former employee's work email addresses after the employment ended in June 2022. The inspectorate asked the company twice, in November and late November 2022, to close them or explain its legal basis, and got no reply. The inspectorate then issued a binding precept (ettekirjutus) ordering the company to close the two addresses by 15 December 2022, and warned of a conditional penalty payment of EUR 2,500 if the order was not met. No administrative fine is imposed in this document.

The Estonian Data Protection Inspectorate opened an own-initiative inquiry in October 2022 into video cameras operated by OÜ Laidoneri KV at Park Hotell Viljandi. The company relied on employees' consent, which the Inspectorate found could not be valid in an employment relationship, and no legitimate interest assessment had been made; the information signs were also inadequate. The Inspectorate found the processing unlawful under Articles 5, 6, 12 and 13 GDPR and issued a binding precept ordering the camera use to stop until a legitimate interest assessment and privacy terms are approved, with a deadline of 20 December 2022. No fine was imposed, but a conditional coercive fine of EUR 2,000 per unmet obligation was warned of.

The Estonian Data Protection Inspectorate issued a binding precept (ettekirjutus) to the debt collector M&M Inkasso OÜ after a complaint that it published individuals' debt data on its website and social media. The Inspectorate found no lawful basis for the publication: it rejected vital interests, did not accept legitimate interests, and found the journalism exemption under the Estonian act not met because there was no public interest. The company was ordered to stop publishing debtors' personal data on its TikTok, Instagram and Facebook accounts unless the person gave voluntary consent, by 20 December 2022. No fine was imposed; a conditional penalty payment of EUR 1,000 was only warned of.

The European Data Protection Board issued a binding decision in a dispute between the Irish data protection authority (the lead authority) and several other authorities of the European Economic Area about Meta’s Facebook service. The dispute concerned whether Meta could rely on the contract legal basis (Article 6(1)(b) GDPR) for behavioural advertising, and whether the Irish draft decision had properly examined consent and special category data. The Board found that Meta had inappropriately relied on Article 6(1)(b) and therefore lacked a legal basis for behavioural advertising, and it added a fairness infringement under Article 5(1)(a). It instructed the Irish authority to order compliance within three months, to carry out a new investigation into special category data, to set a significantly higher fine for the transparency infringements, and to cover the additional infringement of Article 6(1) GDPR with an administrative fine. The Board itself sets no fine amount.

This is a binding decision of the European Data Protection Board, issued on a dispute raised by the Irish data protection authority and several other authorities over a complaint about Instagram’s processing for behavioural advertising. The Board found that Meta Platforms Ireland could not rely on contractual necessity (Article 6(1)(b) GDPR) for behavioural advertising, so it infringed Article 6(1) GDPR. It also instructed the Irish authority to add a finding of unfairness under Article 5(1)(a), to order compliance within three months, to reassess the fine for the transparency breaches upwards, and to cover the additional infringement of Article 6(1) GDPR with an administrative fine. The Board further required a new investigation into whether special categories of data are processed, and it did not itself set a fine amount.

This is a binding decision of the European Data Protection Board under Article 65 GDPR, issued after the Irish supervisory authority's draft decision on a complaint against WhatsApp Ireland was objected to by six other supervisory authorities of the European Economic Area. The Board found that WhatsApp Ireland could not rely on Article 6(1)(b) GDPR (contract) for service improvement and security processing, and so infringed Article 6(1) GDPR. It also required a finding of an infringement of the fairness principle in Article 5(1)(a) GDPR, an order to bring the processing into compliance, further investigation of several processing purposes, and an administrative fine. The Board did not set any fine amount; that is left to the Irish authority's final decision.

A complainant objected that the municipal social services sent a registered letter to the father of her eldest child (who did not hold custody of the other children). The letter contained her sensitive health information, including a suicide attempt and addiction problems, and the full names and national ID numbers of three of her other children. Persónuvernd found that disclosing her sensitive data had a lawful basis under the child protection act and was compatible with the GDPR. It found that disclosing the other children's names and ID numbers had no legal basis and breached the law.

A complainant asked Íslensk erfðagreining ehf., which runs the genealogy database Íslendingabók jointly with Friðrik Skúlason ehf., to erase her and her minor child's data from the database and website. The company refused. The Authority found that the company could lawfully refuse under Article 17(3)(d) GDPR, because the processing serves historical and scientific research, and that erasure was therefore not required. It also held that the processing could not rest on the public-interest basis in Article 6(1)(e) without a law setting it out, but could rest on legitimate interests under Article 6(1)(f). The complaint was rejected.

The Authority examined a set of complaints and breach notifications about third parties fraudulently obtaining SIM card replacements (SIM swaps), call diversions and new numbers on Vodafone subscribers' lines. It found that the identity-verification policies Vodafone applied over four successive periods were inadequate, that its own policies were sometimes not applied, and that at least five breaches were notified late, after delays of 2-3 months up to over six months. It rejected the ne bis in idem objection based on separate sanctions by the communications privacy authority (ADAE). It imposed a fine of EUR 150,000 for infringing Article 12 of Law 3471/2006.

The Authority examined a series of complaints and breach notifications about unauthorised SIM card replacements and call diversions or new phone numbers obtained by third parties posing as subscribers. It found that Cosmote's security policies in several periods were deficient, that its identity checks were not adequate to prevent abuse, and that its policies were not always applied. It also found that at least eight incidents were not notified to the Authority without delay. The Authority imposed a fine of EUR 150,000 for these infringements of Article 12 of Law 3471/2006. The Authority examined the case in its plenary session of 21 July 2022; the decision document is dated 2 December 2022.

A data subject complained that the company had passed her personal data to the National Revenue Agency (NAP) for a labour contract she never signed. The company had only received her CV, consent form and a job offer that only she, not the employer, had signed, during a recruitment process. The Commission found that the earlier pre-contract processing was lawful, but that filing the labour-contract notice with NAP had no legal basis under Article 6(1). The company had withdrawn the notice 12 days later, and the Commission issued an official warning instead of a fine.

The Italian DPA fined the Lazio Region EUR 100,000 for monitoring the email metadata of staff in the regional legal department (avvocatura), including those writing to a specific trade union. The data was kept for 180 days for generic IT security purposes and used without a proper legal basis, breaching data protection principles and the rules on remote monitoring of workers. The Region said it ran an internal check over a suspected leak of confidential information. The Garante also banned further processing of such metadata and ordered deletion of what was unlawfully collected. This is a press release; the decision itself (1 December 2022) is a separate document.

After a municipal police report and a Guardia di Finanza inspection, the Garante found that two grocery shops ran working CCTV cameras without information signs and without the labour-inspectorate authorisation or union agreement required for cameras that can monitor employees. The owner also failed to answer the Garante's requests for information. Her defence that she acted in good faith and later put up signs and applied for authorisation was not backed by any documents. The Garante declared the processing unlawful, fined the sole trader EUR 6,000 and ordered her to bring the processing into compliance within 60 days. The decision is to be published.

After a local police inspection on 13 April 2022 found video cameras inside and outside a food and drink business, the Garante examined the case. It found that only one hidden information sign was placed inside, none outside, and that the cameras had been installed without the union agreement or Labour Inspectorate authorisation required by Article 4 of Law 300/1970. The Garante imposed a fine of EUR 3,000 for breaches of Articles 5(1)(a) and 13 GDPR and Article 114 of the Italian Privacy Code. It also ordered the business to fix proper signage and comply with Article 4 of Law 300/1970 within 60 days, and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website.

An employee of a hospital company complained that two of its resolutions, one containing his disability status (health data), were published on the institutional website's online notice board and indexed by search engines. The Garante found no legal basis for disseminating the data and noted the ban on disseminating health data. The publication also ran beyond the 15-day limit, partly because of a platform bug. It declared the processing unlawful and fined the company EUR 6,000, with publication of the decision. No corrective measures were ordered because the conduct had ceased.

A former employee of Amazon Italia Logistica complained that the company never answered his access request for professional training certificates held from his employment. The company replied only after the Garante opened its investigation, sending the one certificate it could obtain and explaining that the others did not exist. The Garante rejected the company's excuses (request did not cite Article 15, a dedicated email address was not used, summer holidays) and found breaches of Articles 12 and 15 GDPR. It imposed a fine of EUR 20,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

Police inspecting a jewellery shop found an operating CCTV system with three indoor and two outdoor cameras and no privacy notice. The trader did not submit any defence or documents during the proceedings. The Garante found breaches of the transparency principle in Art. 5(1)(a) and of the information duty in Art. 13 GDPR. It fined the sole trader EUR 2,000 and ordered signage to be installed.

The CNIL restricted committee sanctioned a fixed-line telecoms operator (the published decision withholds its name; the name on this page comes from the CNIL press release) after complaints about subscriber access and erasure requests and a 2019 data breach in which about 4,100 recycled devices were re-issued with the previous subscriber's data still on them. The committee found failures under GDPR Articles 12, 15, 17, 32 and 33, and dropped the alleged consent breach for direct marketing under Article L.34-5 CPCE and Article 7(1) GDPR. It imposed a EUR 300,000 administrative fine, an injunction on source-of-data access requests with a EUR 500 per day penalty, and publication of the decision.

The Polish DPA imposed a €9,738 fine on a law firm for unlawfully processing personal data of potential clients, including data relating to health, in violation of Articles 5(1)(a), 6(1) and 9(2) GDPR.

A complainant, through her lawyer, complained that Advania Ísland ehf., which runs the Signet e-signature service, showed her national ID number and email address to all Signet users and subscribers without time limit. Persónuvernd found that consent given by ticking the terms of use was not valid, and that Advania's legitimate interest did not outweigh the complainant's interests for publishing her email address. For the ID number it found a legitimate interest in subscribers checking recipients via the national register, but held that data minimisation was not met because all users had access, so the publication breached the Act. It ordered Advania to stop displaying users' email addresses and to confirm this by 3 January 2023.

The Irish Data Protection Commission examined how Meta Platforms Ireland Ltd (MPIL) designed its default settings for the Facebook and Messenger search features, which allowed phone numbers and email addresses to be scraped and a dataset of about 533 million users to be published. The inquiry was opened on its own initiative in April 2021. The DPC found infringements of Article 25(1) and Article 25(2) GDPR (data protection by design and by default), and imposed two fines totalling €265 million (€150 million and €115 million), together with an order to bring processing into compliance and a reprimand.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation into OTP Leasing Romania IFN SA in November 2022. It began after the company notified a personal data breach: a person had gained unauthorised access to the MyLeasing platform by altering the URL and creating an administrator account. The data of contact persons of corporate clients (names, email addresses, phone numbers) could be accessed. The authority found that the controller lacked adequate technical and organisational measures, did not regularly test their effectiveness, and did not inform the affected individuals. It fined the company RON 14,675.7 (about EUR 3,000).

A buyer of a house asked a real estate agency to remove from its website the listing of the property he had just bought, including its postal address, cadastral parcel numbers, photos and Google Maps view. The agency refused and kept the listing for marketing. The Belgian DPA's Litigation Chamber issued a prima facie decision finding that the agency had likely breached the GDPR: it did not answer the erasure and objection requests or inform the buyer in time, it had no lawful basis under Article 6 (the legitimate-interests test failed on necessity and balancing), and it did not notify the recipients of the erasure. It ordered the agency to comply with the erasure and objection requests and the notification duty within 30 days, and issued a warning. No fine was imposed.

The Romanian authority published a press release announcing that, after an investigation completed in November 2022, it fined Medicover S.R.L. The investigation began with a personal data breach notification from the company. An email sent to a client contained additional annexes of medical service contracts belonging to other clients, leading to unauthorised disclosure of names, national ID numbers (CNP), addresses and signatures. The authority found that the company had not implemented adequate technical and organisational measures under Article 32 GDPR and imposed a fine of RON 4,901, stated as the equivalent of EUR 1,000.

The CNIL restricted committee fined a large French electricity and energy company, whose name is redacted in the text, EUR 600,000 for breaches of the French electronic marketing rules and several GDPR provisions. The breaches concerned failure to prove prospects' consent to marketing calls and texts when their data came from data brokers, and deficiencies in the information given to data subjects, including retention periods and data sources. Complaints about the exercise of data subject rights, from August 2019 to December 2020, led to the inquiry. The committee took account of the company's compliance measures and the limited, non-structural nature of the breaches, ordered no compliance injunction, and ordered publication of the decision.

A customer complained that the electricity distributor Areti wrongly flagged him as a defaulting customer (CMOR indemnity) in the integrated information system, and that his access request was answered inadequately. The Garante investigated and found that a faulty data-extraction query and an erroneous data migration produced inaccurate data for thousands of people over about five years. It found breaches of the accuracy and storage limitation principles, accountability, transparency/access rights and controller obligations. It fined Areti EUR 1,000,000 and ordered it to correct the wrongly migrated data and annotate the records.

A customer complained that a roadside assistance company, collected her personal data during a breakdown service without giving her a proper privacy notice. The Garante found that the 'Scheda lavoro' form only contained a generic line authorising processing, with none of the information required by Article 13, and that the website notice was outdated and covered only browsing data and cookies. The company updated its notices during the proceedings. The Garante found infringements of Articles 5(1)(a) and 13 GDPR, imposed a fine of EUR 1,000 and ordered publication of the decision on its website.

Two complainants objected that a specialisation thesis by a psychologist, published on a website, described their family history and psychotherapy in a way that let them be identified, with names of them and their children, ages, professions and workplaces. The Garante found that the publication was processing health data and personal data without any legal basis under Articles 6 and 9, that removing surnames did not amount to anonymisation, and that security measures under Article 32 were inadequate. Because the thesis had already been removed, no corrective measures were ordered, but a EUR 1,000 fine was imposed and the decision was ordered published on the Garante's website.

A doctor employed by the regional health agency complained that the Cagliari medical association, after the agency suspended him for not meeting the COVID-19 vaccination requirement, forwarded the full suspension documents, including the agency's assessment and annexes, to several public bodies under a 1950 decree. The Garante found that the association had no legal basis for communicating the complete documents and lacked a proper assessment of their necessity and relevance. It issued a fine of EUR 3,000 and ordered publication of the decision on its website.

A sports-medicine clinic told a gym, where the complainant had enrolled, that her non-competitive sports fitness certificate was suspended pending further tests. The gym then denied her access. The Garante held that this news reveals health information and was disclosed without a legal basis or the complainant's consent, breaching Articles 5 and 9 GDPR. It fined the company EUR 4,000 and ordered publication of the decision. No corrective measures were imposed because the conduct had ended and a DPO had been appointed.

An individual complained that Gallup had stored his home phone number in its internal phone-number database to use for survey recruitment calls. Gallup relied on legitimate interests. After Gallup called his wife, the complainant objected, and Gallup then flagged both of them in the database so they would not be contacted again. Persónuvernd found that Gallup had a legitimate interest, that the processing was fair and transparent, and that Gallup had handled the objection adequately under Article 21, so the processing complied with the GDPR and the Icelandic Act No. 90/2018.

A teacher complained that the school had collected information about her from colleagues and passed it to the Ministry of Education and to the Parliamentary Ombudsman without her consent and without informing her. The Authority dismissed the part of the complaint about the transfer to the Ombudsman, because the Ombudsman's work falls outside the GDPR and the Act. On the rest, it found that the school's processing complied with the data protection rules: the collection was part of the employer-employee relationship, the transfer to the Ministry was a legal duty, and the information duty in Article 14 did not apply because the data did not come from a third party. No infringement was found.

The Icelandic DPA held that a school administrator did not breach the GDPR when sharing the teaching evaluation of a data subject with other staff in a meeting, as the administrator could base the processing on Article 6(1)(c) GDPR and did not share the data with any unauthorized parties.

A complainant's mobile phone number was assigned by Nova hf. to a third party who had applied for a new number, so the complainant's number went dead and became active on the third party's phone. Persónuvernd found that Nova did not ensure the security of the complainant's personal data as required by Article 32 GDPR and the Icelandic Data Protection Act, and that the incident was a personal data breach which Nova should have reported to the authority and the data subject. Persónuvernd issued an order requiring Nova to take measures so that numbers already in use cannot be reassigned, with confirmation due by 21 December 2022. No fine was imposed.

A complainant alleged that RTBF's website placed non-essential cookies, including targeted advertising and social network cookies, before consent was given. The Inspection Service found such cookies were set when the homepage opened. The Dispute Chamber dismissed the complaint on technical grounds under Article 100(1)(1) WOG. Its settlement decision 168/2022, taken the same day against RTBF for the same facts, covered 25 May 2018 to 11 November 2020, and it found no basis for findings after 20 November 2020. No fine or order was imposed in this decision.

A company complained that the Public Employment Service (AMS) had, without consent, taken job advertisements from its website and republished them on the AMS job platform 'JobRoboter', infringing its right to confidentiality. The DSB held that the data were generally available and, in any case, AMS had a statutory basis for publishing them as part of its job-placement tasks, so the complaint was dismissed. A supplementary complaint about the right of access was rejected as a new subject matter raised too late.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation in October 2022 into ING Bank NV Amsterdam Bucharest Branch, started after the bank notified a personal data breach. Customer data, including identity, contact and banking details and Internet Banking credentials, were accessed and disclosed without authorisation, and third parties made payment operations. The authority found the bank had not implemented appropriate technical and organisational security measures, in breach of Article 32(1) and (2) GDPR. It imposed a fine of RON 98,076, equal to EUR 20,000, which was paid. The press release also says Raiffeisen Bank SA paid its fine.
The Belgian DPA ordered a Covid-19 contact tracking centre to answer an access request, to which the centre did not reply.

After a complaint from an individual, the authority investigated a homeowners association whose president had shared video surveillance recordings showing the complainant in the block's WhatsApp group. The association did not supply the information the authority requested within the legal deadline. The authority found a breach of Article 58(1) GDPR, with Article 83(5)(e), and fined the association 1,480.98 lei (about EUR 300).

During the COVID-19 emergency in spring 2020, two camera cars were used in Rotterdam to monitor and enforce corona rules, filming public spaces including identifiable adults and children. The police chief had not carried out a data protection impact assessment before the processing began; a pre-assessment concluding none was needed was only adopted on 10 May 2020, and the actual assessment on 26 May 2020, while filming continued. The Dutch DPA found a breach of Article 4c(1) of the Police Data Act. It set a fine of EUR 50,000, reduced from the base amount of EUR 56,500 because of the exceptional crisis circumstances at the start of the pandemic.

The Belgian DPA's Litigation Chamber examined the Flemish tourism agency Toerisme Vlaanderen, which requested host and accommodation data from Airbnb through random 'sondages' (spot checks), and did so without consulting its data protection officer. The Chamber's operative part finds violations of the transparency, accountability, privacy-by-design and DPO-involvement provisions (Articles 12 to 14, 5(2), 24(1), 25(1), 38(1) and 39(1) GDPR) and issues a reprimand. The other findings, including the Article 5(1)(a) and (c) and Article 6(1) lawfulness findings, are dismissed. No administrative fine is imposed because the Chamber cannot fine public bodies.

The Romanian authority finished an investigation in September 2022 at Raiffeisen Bank SA, started after the bank sent 17 personal data breach notifications. Findings included unsigned credit bureau queries, prescoring for an external broker, credits granted to clients who had not requested them, suspected internal fraud, emails with client documents sent to wrong recipients, and disclosure of Smart Mobile account data to other clients. The bank was sanctioned with three fines totalling RON 138,572 (about EUR 28,000) and two warnings, under Articles 32 and 25(1) GDPR.

The Polish DPA fined the company that took over Virgin Mobile (its legal successor), PLN 1,599,395 for Virgin Mobile's breach: lack of appropriate technical and organisational measures, which resulted in a data breach affecting over 114,000 persons. It was the DPA's second decision in the case: on 21 October 2021 the Warsaw Administrative Court had annulled the first, of 3 December 2020 (2020/PL/005).

A healthcare provider reported to the Finnish Data Protection Ombudsman that a bag was stolen from a parked car. The bag held a laptop protected only by a password, two unencrypted external hard drives with customer data, and paper records including patient documents. About 3,000 data subjects were affected, and the data included health information. The Deputy Data Protection Ombudsman found that the controller had not complied with Article 32(1) and (2) GDPR and issued a reprimand under Article 58(2)(b). No fine was imposed.

According to the Slovenian DPA, sending emails containing personal data to unauthorized recipients constitutes unlawful processing under Article 6(1) GDPR. However the authority found a mitigating circumstance since most of the recipients were bound by professional secrecy.

A parent who is not the guardian of a minor child asked the hospital district to correct and delete the child's patient records, saying they did not match the facts. The documents show that a court had confirmed the parent's right of access to the child's information, but the parent is not the child's guardian or other legal representative. The Deputy Data Protection Ombudsman held that this right of access did not make the parent a data subject or the child's representative under the GDPR, so the parent could not claim the rights to correction and deletion (Articles 16 and 17) for the child. The request was rejected, and there was no reason to consider an order.

The French CNIL restricted committee fined a company, whose name is redacted in the text, EUR 800,000 after an online inspection in November 2020 and a follow-up document inspection. The company ran a voice and chat platform with user accounts. The committee found breaches of Art. 5(1)(e) (indefinite retention of inactive accounts), Art. 13 (generic retention information), and also Arts. 25(2) (data protection by default), 32 (a password policy that was not robust enough) and 35 (no impact assessment before the processing began). It found the company had since adopted a retention policy but still treated the breach as established. It also ordered publication of the decision, with the company's name removed after two years.

An 85-year-old woman was called by a call centre in Vodafone's sales network and, she says unknowingly, concluded a fixed-line contract by voice recording. Her son complained to the Garante. The Garante found that Vodafone could not show valid consent to the promotional contact, that the consent formula was undifferentiated and read out too fast to be understood, that no proper information notice was given, and that the contract was presented in breach of fairness and transparency. It banned further processing of the complainant's data and fined Vodafone EUR 500,000, with publication of the decision.

The Garante fined the only health authority of Valle d'Aosta EUR 40,000. During the Covid-19 emergency it had removed the privacy filters on its corporate health dossier by an administrative act, so any health worker could open the dossiers of all patients in the region, whatever their consent or whether they treated them. It also had no measures to detect abnormal access. The case began with a complaint from a health worker who had refused consent to the dossier but whose file was repeatedly accessed by a colleague who had never treated her. The Garante said the Covid rules did not override the general principles and rules for health data in dossiers. This text is a newsletter summary, not the decision itself.

A municipal employee complained that the municipality published on its online notice board, and then in its historical archive, an executive decision containing his name, the amount withheld from his salary for a loan repayment (cessione del quinto), the duration and the bank's IBAN. The Garante found there was no suitable legal basis for publishing this data and that the principles of lawfulness and data minimisation were breached. The publication also stayed online beyond the 15-day period because of an automatic archiving function. It fined the municipality EUR 4,000 and ordered publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were needed because the dissemination had ended.

A trade union reported that the company, which runs gyms in Milan, had introduced fingerprint-based time clocks for all employees. The Garante asked the company for information twice without any reply, then inspected it in September 2021. It found fingerprint processing of about 132 employees from October 2018 until 2 May 2022, relying on consent in a general employee notice, with minimal information and a processing register that omitted biometric data. The Garante found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a), 9, 13 and 30(1)(c) GDPR and of Article 157 of the Code (failure to answer its requests), and fined the company EUR 20,000, with publication of the decision.

A man complained that I-Model s.r.l. only formally answered his two erasure requests: it confirmed deletion but kept sending him job-offer SMS messages. The Garante found that the company had given a merely formal reply and kept processing his data without a legal basis after consent was withdrawn. It found violations of Articles 17 and 6(1) GDPR and imposed a fine of EUR 10,000, and ordered publication of the decision on its website.

Two complainants objected that the municipality of Cisterna di Latina disclosed their personal data to third parties (excess data, including an identity document) when handling access-to-documents requests, and did not answer their data subject access requests. It also emerged that the municipality had no data protection officer for several months after the first one resigned. The Garante found breaches of data minimisation (Art. 5(1)(c)), Art. 12 and Art. 37(1)(a), but closed the complaint about the late communication of the first DPO's contact details as an excusable error. It fined the municipality EUR 5,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

A student complained that the music conservatory had obtained the recording of an online student assembly, had it transcribed, and used his statements to open disciplinary proceedings against him. The Garante found that the conservatory processed the recording without a valid legal basis and in breach of the principles of lawfulness and purpose limitation. It also found that the conservatory had appointed its Director as data protection officer, which is a conflict of interest. A fine of EUR 6,000 was imposed and the decision is to be published. No corrective measures were ordered because the conduct had ceased.

A patient complained that at a radiology clinic she was asked to sign on a tablet for privacy without seeing any text, and that no DPO contact details were given. The Garante found the privacy information incomplete (no right to complain, no retention period or criteria, no DPO contact) and that no compliant DPO had been designated. It fined the company EUR 15,000 for breaching Articles 5, 13 and 37 GDPR, ordered it to complete the notice and designate and publish a DPO, and ordered publication of the decision.

Romania's data protection authority finished an investigation in October 2022 into SC Das Sense Society SRL. The investigation followed complaints that surveillance cameras at the operator's premises filmed public areas (pavement and street) and private areas (a ramp and access stairs to a housing complex, the entrance to a supermarket). The operator did not respond to the authority's request for information, so the authority found a breach of Article 58(1) GDPR. It imposed a fine of 4,950 lei, stated to be equivalent to EUR 1,000.

A data subject who had rented a registered office and mail-handling service from a company asked it on 27 June 2021 for access to his personal data and related information. The company did not respond within the one-month deadline, and it also ignored two warnings from the authority. The authority issued a penal order finding a breach of the right of access under Article 15(1) GDPR, imposing a fine of CZK 10,000 at the bottom of the statutory range, and ordering the company to grant the access and provide the missing information and report back.

The Icelandic DPA rejected the complaint of a data subject based on Article 17 GDPR against Google LLC to remove search results containing their personal data, because their interests were outweighed the right of freedom of expression and information pursuant to Article 17(3)(a) GDPR.

An individual complained about credit scoring by Creditinfo, about Netgíró ehf. withdrawing his credit facility based on that score without prior notice, and about ÍL-sjóður reporting an allegedly already-paid debt to Creditinfo's debt-status system. Persónuvernd found that Creditinfo's processing, ÍL-sjóður's disclosure and Netgíró's processing all complied with the Icelandic data protection act and the GDPR. No infringement was found, so no fine or order was imposed.

A complainant who works in IT was repeatedly called by the controller and asked for his data to be erased, without any result. On 16 August 2022 he also sent an access request under Article 15 and an erasure request under Article 17, and received no reply to either. The Litigation Chamber issued a prima facie decision, not a decision on the merits, finding that the absence of any response breached Articles 12(3), 15(1) and 17(1) GDPR. It ordered the controller to grant access and erase the data within 30 days and to inform the Chamber; no fine was imposed. The controller may ask for a merits hearing within 30 days.

A complainant received unsolicited newsletter emails from a controller after he had asked for erasure under Article 17 GDPR and got no reply within one month. The Litigation Chamber examined whether the GDPR applies at all. The controller has no establishment in the EEA, and its English-language workshops and book, sold in dollars and shekels to buyers in the US, Canada and Israel, were not found to target people in the EEA or to monitor their behaviour under Article 3(2). The GDPR was therefore held not to apply and the complaint was dismissed on technical grounds (technisch sepot) under Article 95 §1(3) of the DPA law, with no finding on the merits.

A mother (called A in the decision) complained to Datatilsynet that staff at a child welfare service had looked up her son's child welfare file without a work-related need. On 2 May 2022 Datatilsynet declined to investigate, saying the matter fell outside its competence because the county governor (Statsforvalteren) supervises the child welfare service and had already reviewed the access logs. She appealed to the Privacy Appeals Board (Personvernnemnda), which on 8 November 2022 agreed that Datatilsynet lacked competence under GDPR Article 57(1)(a) and upheld the rejection, without finding any infringement.

The Romanian DPA concluded an investigation in October 2022 into a company that published on its website 23 named decisions terminating employment contracts of people with no legal relationship to it. These contained names, positions, contract numbers and disciplinary offences. The company could not show a lawful basis for the online disclosure. The authority found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a), 5(2) and 6 GDPR, fined the company RON 24,683.5 (about EUR 5,000) and ordered removal or anonymisation of identifying information.

The Belgian DPA warned a controller for publishing an invoice with personal data on Facebook. The controller did not have a legal basis (Article 6 GDPR) and did not delete the invoice after the data subject requested erasure.

A former employee complained that her name, job title and individual photo, and a team photo, stayed on the company's website after she left in February 2022. She asked for their removal by email on 1 September 2022, and nothing had been done when she complained to the APD on 28 September 2022. The Chamber Contentieuse issued a prima facie decision, not a decision on the merits. It ordered the company to comply with the erasure request, including removing the team photo, within 30 days, and issued a warning about the lack of a procedure for departing staff and the one-month response deadline. The company may ask for a merits review within 30 days.

The Romanian data protection authority finished an investigation in October 2022 into Romanian Post, which acted as a processor. The company lost postal items containing pension decisions, work booklets and death certificates, affecting 35 individuals. The authority found it had not put adequate technical and organisational measures in place and breached Article 32(1)(b) and (2) GDPR. It fined the company RON 9,883.80 (about EUR 2,000) and ordered it to review and update its security measures under Article 58(2)(d).

The mayor of a Polish commune reported to UODO the theft of a work laptop from an employee's home. The laptop held a file with name, address and PESEL number for 51 members of an organisation. The mayor's own risk analysis and internal rules required full-disk encryption, but the laptop's hard drive was not encrypted. UODO found breaches of the principles of integrity and confidentiality, accountability, data protection by design, and security of processing, and imposed a fine of PLN 8,000 on the mayor. The decision is marked as final (prawomocna).

The Portuguese DPA reprimanded and fined the municipality of Setubal €170,000 for violations of the integrity and confidentiality principle, the storage limitation principle, the information obligations from Article 13 GDPR and for not appointing a DPO with regard to the collection of personal data of Ukrainian refugees, who were using a helpline in Portugal.

Portugal's data protection authority (CNPD) found that the National Statistical Institute (INE) committed five administrative offences under the GDPR in the 2021 Census and imposed a single combined fine of EUR 4,300,000. It held that INE processed health and religion data unlawfully, because it did not make clear that answering those questions was optional; that it did not meet its duty to inform the people who answered the census questionnaire; that it did not exercise due diligence in choosing its processor, a company based in the United States (Cloudflare, Inc.); that it broke the rules on transfers of data to other countries; and that it did not carry out a data protection impact assessment of the census. During the census the CNPD had already ordered INE to suspend sending census data to the United States and other countries without an adequate level of protection. The final deliberation (2022/1072) is dated 2 November 2022; the CNPD announced it on 12 December 2022.
The Greek DPA examined the Ministry of Education and Religious Affairs compliance with the provisions of the legislation on the processing of personal data with regards to distant learning.

A member of a staff committee complained that a fellow member repeatedly forwarded emails containing his name and work email address to people outside the committee and to union and collective mailboxes, despite his written objections. The AEPD found the processing had no legal basis under Article 6 GDPR, rejected the respondent's argument that Article 9 (union membership data) applied, and rejected his request to annul the proceedings over a notification issue. It imposed a fine of EUR 2,000 for an Article 6 infringement, citing negligence given the respondent's role.

The DPA fined VODAFONE €56,000 for sharing confidential data of another customer while addressing a different customer's right of access. The controller benefitted from a €14,000 reduction in the original fine as they renounced to any form of appeal against the sanction

A complaint was lodged by a law firm on behalf of a car owner after BL ehf. refused a request, made through a company acting under the owner's power of attorney, for the repair and service history of his car. BL ehf. argued that the request was not a formal one from the owner, that it was electronic, and that such records are only issued on paper to a customer who appears in person with ID. The Icelandic DPA held that the handling of the access request did not comply with Act No. 90/2018 and the GDPR, because a request made under a valid power of attorney is equivalent to a request by the data subject, and the controller should have guided the agent on form requirements instead of refusing. BL ehf. was reprimanded and ordered to handle the access request on its merits, with confirmation due by 28 November 2022.
The Spanish Data Protection agency held that the sending of an email regarding personal data to a not authorised recipient infringes Articles 5 and 32 GDPR.

The Danish DPA carried out a written supervision of JP/Politiken's cookie consent solution on www.eb.dk. The first layer offered 'Kun nødvendige', 'Tilpas Indstillinger' and 'Acceptér alle', and the 'preferences' purpose was visible only on a second layer, so visitors who clicked 'Acceptér alle' were not informed about it. The DPA found that consent was therefore not valid under Article 6(1)(a) read with Article 4(11), and that the green-highlighted 'accept all' design breached the principle in Article 5(1)(a). It issued a severe criticism (reprimand) and imposed no fine. The decision covers only the old consent solution, which JP changed during the case.
The Authority, acting unanimously, shall decide to specify the rules for the removal of identification in its decisions posted on its website.

A person reported receiving by certified email the histology report of another patient, sent by mistake by the Careggi hospital in Florence. Careggi acted as processor for I.S.P.R.O., the controller and the regional oncology institute. The Garante found that I.S.P.R.O., as controller, remained responsible and should have supervised its processor. It declared the processing unlawful for breach of Articles 5(1)(f) and 9 GDPR and fined I.S.P.R.O. EUR 7,000, with publication of the decision. No corrective orders were imposed as measures against recurrence had been implemented.

A complainant, a lawyer employed by a foundation, objected that the foundation had published on its 'transparent administration' web page three decisions containing her personal data, including sick certificates and a reference to a precautionary suspension. The Garante found that the foundation had published health data, whose dissemination is expressly prohibited, and information not necessary for the purpose, without a legal basis. It treated the fault as negligent and isolated and took into account the data being blacked out, staff training and cooperation. It imposed a fine of EUR 5,000 and ordered publication of the decision, with no further corrective measures since the conduct had ceased.

A person complained that the Careggi hospital trust sent him by certified email another patient's histological report. The trust acts as processor for ISPRO in this lab activity; a clerk attached the wrong report from a spool folder holding two near-identical names. The Garante found a breach of the confidentiality principle, of Article 9 and of the security obligations in Article 32. It fined the trust EUR 9,000 and ordered publication of the decision, but imposed no corrective orders because the trust had already changed its procedure.

A school institute published on its online notice board (Albo pretorio) a determination ending a permanent teacher's employment contract, together with the attached ministry decision, without anonymising the teacher's personal data. A complaint led to the Garante's investigation. The Garante found the publication unlawful for lack of a legal basis and breach of the data minimisation and lawfulness principles, under Articles 5(1)(a) and (c) and 6 GDPR and the pre-2021 version of Article 2-ter of the Italian Privacy Code. It imposed a fine of EUR 900 and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website.

The Italian Archery Federation published on its website a disciplinary decision against the complainant. It contained data on criminal convictions and offences and stayed online for about five years. The Garante found no suitable legal basis for publishing it. The federation's reliance on the transparency decree was rejected. The Garante also found the five-year retention unjustified and breaches of lawfulness, purpose limitation, minimisation and storage limitation. It fined the federation EUR 10,000. No further corrective measures were ordered, because the federation had already redacted the data and de-indexed the pages after the complaint.

A resident complained that the municipality used video surveillance during the COVID-19 lockdown to detect a lockdown breach, had inadequate signage, and ignored his request for access to the footage. The Garante found the municipality's signage and full privacy notice inadequate, no retention period fixed for images used for administrative purposes, a fee wrongly demanded for access, and no record of processing activities for a period. It declared the processing unlawful, fined the municipality EUR 12,000, ordered it to provide the footage free of charge (or justify refusal) within 30 days, and ordered publication of the decision.

A customer complained that Douglas Italia did not answer her data subject request. The Garante then inspected the company in late 2021 and examined its marketing and profiling processing. It found that the app collected a bundled consent that was neither free nor specific, that the company could not document consents or notices inherited from three merged companies, that the data of about 3.3 million inactive customers were kept without justification, that the privacy notice was incomplete, and that telemarketing by stores lacked procedures. The Garante declared the processing unlawful, ordered corrective measures and deletion of old data, and imposed a fine of EUR 1,400,000, publishing the decision.

The Italian DPA received a complaint that the Policlinico Casilino in Rome let people into its outpatient clinics only if they held a Covid-19 green certificate. The Policlinico argued the check was voluntary and a public-health precaution taken in good faith, and said the practice had ended. The Garante found there was no legal basis in national law for requiring the certificate for outpatient care, so the processing of health data breached the lawfulness and purpose limitation principles and Article 9 GDPR. It fined the Policlinico EUR 30,000 and ordered publication of the decision. The Rome Tribunal later reduced the fine to EUR 15,000 (judgment 8977/2025); the Garante's published text now shows the reduced amount.

The Norwegian Data Protection Authority inspected the Norwegian Correctional Service Directorate and three subordinate units between November 2021 and April 2022, focusing on the processing of personal data in the execution of sentences. It found that responsibility for processing was unclear and that internal control was deficient. By letter of 19 October 2022 it issued two binding orders: clarify responsibilities and authority, and review and update the information security internal control system. It set a six-month deadline, to 19 April 2023, and no fine was imposed.

The UK Information Commissioner issued Interserve Group Limited with a monetary penalty notice under the Data Protection Act 2018 for infringements of Article 5(1)(f) and Article 32 GDPR. The contraventions, in the period from March 2019 to December 2020, left Interserve vulnerable to a cyber attack in spring 2020 that affected the personal data of up to 113,000 employees. The Commissioner imposed a fine of £4,400,000 after adjusting a starting point of £4,000,000.

A complainant, a former employee of an employee association (SSF), asked Landsbankinn for access to emails between bank staff that concerned the association's work and not the bank's business. The bank refused, saying the emails belonged to SSF as a separate controller and the request was not made in good faith. Persónuvernd found that the bank was entitled to refuse access to these emails, because they were not the bank's own processing and SSF was responsible for them.

Two social housing tenants complained that the housing association (called Y in the decision) had passed their personal data to a private investigation firm for a foreign (Turkish) property investigation to check their eligibility for social housing. The Inspection Service also reported findings on the processor contract, transfers to Turkey and the records of processing. The Litigation Chamber accepted that the association could rely on Article 6(1)(e) GDPR as its legal basis. It found a violation of Article 28(2) and (3) GDPR on the processor contract, issued a reprimand, and dismissed the other grievances as manifestly unfounded. No administrative fine was imposed because the association had already remedied the breaches.

The Romanian DPA announced it had finished an investigation into a company that owns the website depozit-online.ro. The investigation began after a complaint that the site's representatives had not acted on a request to delete an account. The company did not provide the information the authority requested in its letters. It was fined RON 9,897.2 (stated as EUR 2,000) for breaching Article 58(1) GDPR, read with Article 83(5). The press release also reports a second, separate fine on a private individual, which is not part of this decision.

This Romanian press release covers two investigations; this entry concerns the second, against a private individual. The individual had access to personal data that had been disclosed accidentally and used them without authorisation and without the consent of the data subject. The authority found a breach of Article 6(1)(a) GDPR and imposed a contravention fine of 729 lei, stated as the equivalent of EUR 150.

A holiday-park owner complained that the park's swimming-pool operator issued a digital membership card for discounted pool access that required a photo of each cardholder and the degree of family relationship to the owner. The Litigation Chamber accepted the contractual basis for the card and the purpose of preventing misuse, and found no breach of Article 6(1) or 13(1)(c). It found that photos and kinship degree were not necessary, since names plus a visual check of the ID card would achieve the same purpose, so Article 5(1)(c) was breached. It ordered the controller to bring the processing into line with Article 5(1)(c) within two months and to inform the authority; no fine was imposed.

The CNIL's restricted committee fined a US company that runs a facial recognition search engine built from billions of images scraped from public websites. The company had not answered access and erasure requests or the CNIL's formal notice of 26 November 2021, and it had no legal basis for its processing. The CNIL imposed a fine of EUR 20,000,000, ordered the company to stop processing data of people in France without a legal basis and to delete that data under a penalty of EUR 100,000 per day of delay, and ordered publication of the decision.

A complainant received a payment demand for electricity bills at an address he said he had never lived at, and asked for his email address to be erased from the databases of two energy-sector companies. He also said his identity had been usurped and had filed complaints with several other bodies. The Chambre Contentieuse dismissed the complaint on grounds of opportunity, because it was ancillary to a wider commercial dispute better handled elsewhere. It recalled the minimisation and storage-limitation principles without finding an infringement, and did not send the decision to the defendants at the complainant's request for anonymity.

A complainant asked the controller how it had obtained his personal data and wanted to erase it. The controller's privacy statement required an identity card before data subjects could exercise their rights, even though the controller had already identified him through his email address for a prior access request. The Litigation Chamber found that requiring an identity document for direct marketing rights breaches the data minimisation principle in Article 5(1)(c) GDPR. It issued a reprimand under Article 58(2)(c) GDPR and asked the controller to adapt its privacy statement and report back within 30 days, failing which the case would go to a full merits hearing.

A complainant, an employee of a school establishment, asked his employer by registered letter of 7 July 2022 for a copy of all his personal data and for information on the processing, under Article 15. No reply came within one month, and the letter was returned. The Litigation Chamber issued a prima facie decision finding that the controller may have breached Articles 15(1) and 15(3), read with Article 12(3), GDPR. It ordered the controller to comply with the access request within 30 days and to report back to the Chamber. The decision is not a merits ruling, and no fine was imposed.

A complainant ordered a product from Trionic's German website, and Trionic sent the order confirmation to a generic info e-mail address at the complainant's e-mail domain after deciding the address was wrong. It also disclosed the complainant's data to an anti-fraud service provider. IMY found that the e-mail disclosure was not necessary under the claimed legal obligation (breach of Article 6(1)), that the anti-fraud disclosure had a legitimate interest basis, and that the information on recipients was too vague (breach of Article 13(1)(e)). IMY found the infringement minor, issued a reprimand and imposed no fine.

A user complained that the online user area of a water utility's website, which handled logins, contact details and invoices, ran over unencrypted http with no SSL certificate. The Garante's own check confirmed it. The utility moved to https after the proceedings began and cooperated. The Garante found breaches of Articles 5(1)(f), 25(1) and 32 GDPR and imposed a fine of EUR 15,000, and ordered publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were needed because the conduct had ended.

The Italian DPA opened an ex officio investigation into the Clubhouse voice social network after press reports, later also receiving a report. The US operator, which has no EU establishment, argued Italy had no jurisdiction but the Garante found the GDPR applicable because the service was offered to people in the EU. It found unlawful processing, including lack of a valid legal basis, transparency and information failings, an inadequate EU representative, missing processor appointments, inadequate security and no data protection impact assessment. It fined the company EUR 2,000,000, ordered corrective measures, banned further direct marketing, profiling and account-information sharing, and ordered publication of the decision.

A volunteer member of a social cooperative resigned and asked in the same letter for his personal data to be erased. The cooperative acknowledged the resignation but did not answer the erasure request within one month, and gave no reasons or information about complaint rights until the Garante intervened. The Garante found a breach of Article 12 in relation to Article 17 GDPR and fined the cooperative EUR 10,000. It also ordered publication of the decision on its website.

A founding member of a civil-protection drone association was expelled and lost access to his association email account, whose password was then changed. He asked repeatedly to recover his mail, citing data protection law, but the association did not respond and argued the content belonged to it. The Garante found a breach of the right of access (Arts. 12 and 15(3) GDPR), ordered the association to answer the access request, and fined it EUR 3,000, taking into account its non-profit nature and the economic context. The decision is also published on the Garante's website.

A woman, as heir of two deceased relatives, complained that Poste Italiane did not answer her access request. Poste admitted a clerical error by an employee delayed the handling of the request; it replied only in January 2022, after requesting documents proving her heir status. The Garante found that Poste breached Article 12(3) and (4) GDPR by not answering within one month nor informing her of the reasons and remedies. It fined Poste EUR 10,000, noting negligence, cooperation and no previous violations. No further order was needed since the access request had been satisfied.

The Italian DPA fined the Veneto Region €100,000 for disclosing the data of 12,580 non-vaccinated health workers outside the regulatory framework provided for by national law, in breach of Articles 5(1)(a) and 6 GDPR.

A man who owns a house complained that a newspaper's online article about a 'lockdown party' showed a photo of his house, which he said identified him and led to harassment. He had asked the newspaper to remove the photo and the article; the newspaper checked with its journalist and said the facts were accurate. The Chamber Contentieuse dismissed the complaint on grounds of opportunity, noting that the complainant's evidence was insufficient to balance the rights under Article 17(3)(a) GDPR and that an inspection investigation was not proportionate. It did not find any GDPR infringement and imposed no fine or order.

The UK DPA imposed a fine of 1,350,000 GBP on a catalogue retailer for violating Articles 9 and 13 GDPR by profiling special category (health) data of their customers based on their product purchases without acquiring consent or informing them about it.

Following its earlier Decision 48/2018 on contactless cards, the Authority checked whether Alpha Bank had informed customers that the chip of older Mastercard debit/credit cards stores a history of recent transactions readable contactlessly. The bank had not informed customers and instead chose to phase out the feature by replacing cards. The Authority found a violation of Article 13 GDPR, considering it deliberate, continuing and affecting a large number of customers. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 20,000.

Following earlier Decision 48/2018 on contactless cards, the Greek DPA checked whether Eurobank had complied with its recommendation to inform cardholders that the chip of older Mastercard cards stores the date and amount of recent transactions, readable contactlessly. The check was prompted by a customer's request. The Authority found that Eurobank had not informed customers and had instead decided to phase out the processing by replacing cards. It found a breach of the Article 13 GDPR information obligation and imposed an administrative fine of EUR 20,000.
