Following earlier complaints about contactless cards, the Authority had in Decision 48/2018 recommended that banks inform customers when their cards keep a history of recent transactions in the chip, readable contactlessly. Piraeus Bank did not inform its customers and instead began gradually replacing cards with the feature deactivated, saying notification would be costly and unnecessary. The Authority found a breach of the information duty in Article 13 GDPR. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 20,000 under Articles 58(2)(i) and 83(5) GDPR.

The Authority examined whether National Bank of Greece had complied with its Decision 48/2018, which recommended informing cardholders that their cards kept a history of recent transactions on the chip, readable contactlessly. It found that the bank had not informed customers about this processing and had instead chosen to phase it out by replacing cards. The Authority found a breach of Article 13 GDPR. It imposed a fine of EUR 20,000 under Article 58(2)(i) in conjunction with Article 83(5).

Spanish DPA held a controller responsible for a data breach since they did not have sufficient measures in place to avoid data breaches. Although some measures were applied, they did not provide an adequate level of protection for sensitive data.

The complainant said the controller had recorded wrong personal data about him and his daughter in a case file, and that his repeated requests in February to April 2020 to correct it got no adequate substantive reply. The Litigation Chamber found that the controller had not answered the rectification requests within the one-month period in Article 12(3) GDPR, so it violated the GDPR. It issued a prima facie decision ordering the controller to comply with the rectification request within 30 days, with a possible merits procedure if the controller objects. No fine was imposed.
The Belgian DPA gave a controller a warning for violating Articles 5(1)(a), 5(1)(b), 5(1)(c), 5(2) and 24(1) GDPR by recording the private space of its neighbours with a security camera.

A customer asked the controller for a full vehicle diagnostic report with freeze frame data, to use in an expert assessment. The controller answered within one month but refused, citing an internal policy against sharing internal documents with third parties outside the car-maker network. The Litigation Chamber held that an internal policy cannot override the customer's right of access and that the refusal breached Article 15(1) and 15(3) GDPR. It issued a prima facie order to grant access within 14 days, subject to the controller's right to request a merits hearing.

A complainant asked the controller on 19 June 2022 to erase his personal data under Article 17(1) GDPR, as set out in the controller's privacy policy. By 8 August 2022 he had received no reply, so he complained to the DPA. The Litigation Chamber found that the controller breached Articles 12(3), 12(4) and 17(1) GDPR by not answering the erasure request within the time limits or telling him what it had done. It issued a prima facie order to comply with the erasure request and erase the data within 30 days, and to report the result to the Chamber. The defendant could ask for a merits hearing within 30 days, which would suspend enforcement.

The Hungarian DPA fined a media provider 10,000,000 HUF (approx. €25,650) for, among other things, failing to properly inform data subjects about the processing on its websites and for confusingly using the term "legitimate interest" without referring to its meaning under the GDPR.

A data subject asked a company's customer service on 26 September 2019 for a copy of all data linked to his two accounts. The company's privacy team later replied that the data had been erased, not copied, and the complainant objected, but no answer followed. The Chamber Contentieuse dismissed the complaint on opportunity grounds (elapsed time, low personal impact, likely human error, and the disproportion of a full examination), without a sanction. It did note, prima facie, breaches of Articles 12(3), 15(1) and 15(3) GDPR, and it reminded the controller of its duties on access requests.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation in August 2022 into the controller Bitfactor SRL, which had notified a personal data breach. A faulty application sending marketing messages to website users exposed the confidentiality of the data of 1,757 people. The authority found that the controller had not put in place appropriate technical and organisational measures and had breached Articles 25(1) and 32(1) and (2) GDPR. It fined the controller RON 9,852.8 (stated as equivalent to EUR 2,000).

A complainant, acting for his minor child, said the operator of a petrol station did not grant his access request for video surveillance footage showing the child. The footage had been kept and passed to the police without the child's knowledge. The Authority found the controller did not act on the access request, did not explain why, and did not inform the data subject of the further processing and disclosure to the police. It imposed a single administrative fine of EUR 3,000.

A landowner in a new development area received a purchase offer for his plot from a property developer, with no information on where the developer got his data. The authority found that a surveying engineer used his access to the electronic land register to identify several hundred owners in two cases and passed the data to the developer. The developer wrote to them without the Article 14 information. The authority fined the developer EUR 50,000 and the surveying engineer EUR 5,000 for unlawful collection and disclosure and breach of information duties. Both accepted the fines and they are final.

A property owner in a new development area received a purchase offer from a property developer without being told where his data came from. The fine office found that a surveying engineer had used his right of automated access to the electronic land register to identify several hundred owners in two cases and passed their data to the developer, who wrote to them without the Article 14 information. The authority fined the developer EUR 50,000 and the surveying engineer EUR 5,000 for unlawful collection and disclosure of data and breaches of information duties. Both fines were accepted and are final.

Following two personal data breach notifications from the controller, the Romanian authority investigated a publisher. One breach was a customer database file posted on a public forum; the other was a ransomware attack affecting about 100 employees and collaborators. The authority found the controller had not implemented appropriate technical and organisational security measures. It fined the controller 24,566 lei (about EUR 5,000) under Article 32 GDPR and ordered it to review and update its security measures.

A parent complained that the headteacher of a compulsory school had entered a false attendance record for his child in the Mentor system on the evening of 22 September 2021, allegedly on purpose to affect a custody case. The Authority could not decide whether the entry was intentional or a mistake. The school admitted the record was wrong, and it was corrected about 12 hours later, so the Authority found that the entry breached the accuracy requirement. It did not order the school to take any corrective measures.

The Berlin data protection authority fined a subsidiary of a Berlin e-commerce group EUR 525,000 because its data protection officer had a conflict of interest. He was also managing director of two group service companies that process personal data on behalf of the company he was supposed to supervise. The authority had issued a warning in 2021, and a later check showed the situation continued, so it imposed the fine. The fine was not yet final at the time of the press release.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation into Banca Comercială Română SA after the bank notified a personal data breach. A technical error in an IT application caused emails containing some clients' personal and financial data to be sent to other clients, affecting 564 people. The authority found the bank had not applied adequate technical and organisational measures and breached Articles 25(1) and 32(1)(b), (d) and (2) GDPR. It imposed a fine of 9,864.8 lei (about EUR 2,000).

A complainant reported that the company had posted on Instagram a photo of her in her wedding dress, with her face covered by a black circle, to pursue payment for the dress. The company argued the images were not personal data, that the complainant had tagged it, and that it had a legitimate interest. The AEPD held the images were identifiable, that non-payment did not justify using them without consent, and that the processing had no legal basis under Article 6 GDPR. It imposed a fine of EUR 10,000 for infringing Article 6.

A mother complained that the Rieti local health authority had sent her daughter, who died in 1995, an invitation to a cervical cancer screening programme. The Garante found that the regional screening database (SIPSOweb), run by Lazio Region, held outdated data, and that the Region had not correctly identified the roles of the parties involved, the legal bases for the processing, or the information to give to data subjects. It declared the processing unlawful, ordered the Region to correct roles, purposes, legal bases and information notices within 90 days, and fined it EUR 100,000. The decision is also to be published on the Garante's website.

The Municipal Police of Milan reported a video surveillance system with four cameras at a residential building owned by the company, installed at the request of some tenants. A Guardia di Finanza inspection found only a camera pictogram at the entrance, with no information on the controller or the purposes of processing. The company did not respond to the Garante's notice of the proceedings or send any defence submissions. The Garante found a breach of the transparency principle (Art. 5(1)(a)) and of the information duty (Art. 13), imposed a fine of EUR 2,000, and ordered the company to install suitable information signs.

A former job candidate and employee complained that the bank did not answer his erasure requests on time or properly. His January 2019 request was never actioned because of an internal mishap, and the reply to his lawyer's later requests came only on 17 June 2019, about four months after the legal deadline. The bank also failed to tell him he could complain to the authority or go to court when it declined to erase data it lawfully kept. The Garante found a breach of Article 12 in connection with Article 17 and fined the bank EUR 10,000, with publication of the decision.

A complainant, a former municipal employee dismissed after disciplinary proceedings, complained that the municipality published on its online notice board (albo pretorio) a determination recording the dismissal, identified by staff number, from 17 to 31 October 2019. The Garante held that the staff number made the person identifiable, that no law required publishing the dismissal, and that the publication breached the principles of lawfulness and data minimisation and lacked a legal basis. It imposed a fine of EUR 3,000 and ordered publication of the decision on its website. It archived the complaint about the press release, which contained no personal data.

An employee complained that FCA Italy never answered his formal access request of January 2021 for the data in his personnel file and related work records. The company said it intended to reply in a face-to-face meeting that was repeatedly postponed, and that much of the data was already available to him through an intranet platform and a phone service. The Garante held that the company should have replied in writing within the legal deadline, and that data already held by the person can still be requested. It found breaches of Articles 12 and 15 GDPR and fined the company EUR 40,000, taking into account a previous similar finding against it.

The Irish DPC examined a complaint, referred to it by the Berlin DPA, that Airbnb Ireland UC required a photo ID copy to verify the identity of a user asking for account erasure. The complainant's access request sent after deletion was also not handled in time. The DPC found that the ID requirement breached data minimisation under Article 5(1)(c), that legitimate interest was not a valid basis under Article 6(1) for that ID request, and that the access request response breached Article 12(3). It found no undue delay on the erasure request. No fine was imposed; the DPC issued a reprimand and ordered Airbnb to revise its erasure-request procedures.

The Swedish authority IMY examined Verifiera AB, which runs a website offering searchable court rulings in psychiatric and forced-care (LVM) cases since 2008. It found that between 6 April and 28 June 2022 the company processed health data without a valid legal basis under Article 9: explicit consent was collected only after the data had been published, and neither the freedom of expression nor the public access principle could justify the processing. IMY issued a reprimand and ordered the company to stop allowing searches by name, personal number or address that return these rulings. No fine was imposed, because of the special constitutional media protection of the website and because the new rule limiting it had never been applied.
